hello.note: Respectful, often with palms pressed together. Friends usually just say 'hai'.

goodbye.note: Lit. 'I'll go and come back', said by the one leaving; a bare 'I'm going' sounds final.

please.note: Formal. In speech politeness usually comes from the ending -amo? ('could you?'), e.g. tharamo?

thank_you.note: Spelled nandi but said nanni. Thank you very much: valare nanni (വളരെ നന്ദി).

youre_welcome.note: Lit. 'What of it?', i.e. it was nothing. There is no set reply; saramilla ('it's nothing') is also common.

yes.note: Casual: um (ഉം). A sideways tilt of the head also means yes or OK.

no.note: To turn down something offered, say venda (വേണ്ട, 'I don't want it').

sorry.note: For small slips, the English 'sorry' is very common in everyday speech.

excuse_me.note: To a woman: ചേച്ചീ, ഒന്നു ചോദിച്ചോട്ടെ? (chechee, onnu chodichotte?). Chetta/chechi = elder brother/sister.

good_morning.note: Formal, heard on radio and TV. Face to face, most people say 'good morning' in English.

how_are_you.note: Friendly, to someone you know: enthokkeyundu vishesham? ('What's new?')

im_fine.note: Often just sukham. To ask back: ningalkko? ('And you?')

whats_your_name.note: Very formal: thankalude instead of ningalude. Casual: perentha?

where_from.note: Between Malayalis the usual question is nadu evideya? ('Where's your home town?')

im_from.note: Nadu means home country or home town. This pattern needs no case ending on the place name.

speak_english.note: Lit. 'Do you know English?', the usual way to ask.

speak_slowly.note: The ending -amo? ('could you?') makes it a polite request. Pathukke also means 'softly'.

why.note: In speech often enthina? ('what for?') or enthe?

who.note: In speech usually ആരാ? (ara?), e.g. at the door: 'Who is it?'

how_much.note: Also: ithinu entha vila? ('What's its price?')

where_bathroom.note: 'Toilet' (ടോയ്‌ലറ്റ്) is just as common. Public signs may say ശൗചാലയം.

can_you_help.note: Onnu ('just a bit') softens a request.

one.note: Before a noun it becomes oru: oru chaya (one tea). Old Malayalam digit: ൧.

two.note: Malayalam digit: ൨ (rarely used today; 2 is standard).

seven.note: zh is ഴ, said with the tongue curled back, somewhere between r and l. Digit: ൭

ten.note: The old sign for ten is ൰; today it is written 10.

water.note: Cold water: thanuttha vellam. Eateries often serve warm herbal water by default.

tea.note: Comes with milk and sugar; black tea is kattan chaya (കട്ടൻ ചായ).

bread.note: Means loaf bread; 'bread' (ബ്രെഡ്) is also common. Flatbreads have their own names: chapathi, porotta.

menu_please.note: Small eateries may have no menu: ask enthokke undu? ('What is there?')

bill_please.note: Also common: ethrayayi? ('How much has it come to?')

no_meat.note: Fish and egg don't count as irachi. To rule them out too: njan vejitteriyan anu.

enjoy_meal.note: There is no set 'bon appétit'; hosts urge guests to eat like this. Lit. 'Eat well!'

left.note: To a driver: idatthottu (ഇടത്തോട്ട്, 'to the left').

right.note: To a driver: valatthottu (വലത്തോട്ട്, 'to the right').

stop_here.note: Lit. 'Stopping here is enough', the usual line to taxi and auto drivers.

airport.note: In everyday speech most people say eyarporttu (എയർപോർട്ട്).

hotel.note: In Kerala hottal often means a restaurant; for a place to stay people also say lodge or 'room'.

want_to_go.note: Vare means 'as far as'; it works with any place name, no case ending needed.

is_it_far.note: Can I walk there?: nadannu pokan pattumo?

one_ticket.note: On a bus, just tell the conductor the stop and the number, e.g. 'Aluva, onnu'.

cheaper.note: To bargain: kurachu kuraykkamo? ('Can you bring it down a bit?')

id_like_this.note: Lit. 'This will do for me.' Also: ithu edukkam ('I'll take this').

pay_card.note: Lit. 'Do you take card?' Phone payments are more common: UPI undo?

cash.note: I'll pay cash: kashayi tharam. Formal word: panam (പണം).

open.note: Shop signs are mostly in English. To ask: thurannittundo? ('Is it open?')

big.note: On its own ('a big one'): valuthu (വലുത്).

small.note: On its own ('a small one'): cheruthu (ചെറുത്).

yesterday.note: Keep them apart: innu (today), innale (yesterday), nale (tomorrow).

now.note: In speech: ippo. Right now: ippo thanne.

good_evening.note: Formal. In person most people say namaskaram or 'good evening'.

good_night.note: Formal. Family and friends usually say 'good night' in English.

wait_moment.note: Very common in speech: oru minute! The -e ending makes it a gentle request.

help.note: Ayyo! is the all-purpose cry of alarm and will also bring people running.

im_lost.note: Lit. 'The way went wrong for me.'

dont_feel_well.note: Also very common: enikku vayya (എനിക്ക് വയ്യ, 'I'm not up to it').

allergic.note: The item goes in unchanged, e.g. enikku podi alarjiyanu (dust).

no_problem.note: Also: saramilla ('never mind'), the usual reply to an apology.

i_like_it.note: On first trying something: enikku ishtamayi ('I've taken to it').

dont_like_it.note: Softer: athra ishtamayilla ('I didn't like it much').

im_happy.note: Enikku ('to me') phrases stay the same whether a man or a woman says them.

welcome.note: Swagatham (സ്വാഗതം) is for signs and speeches; at the door hosts say this.
